title: Remembering the Way Out of Egypt
overview: As Israel leaves Egypt, God sets up ways to remember the escape for generations and personally leads the people into the desert.

parts.label: Every firstborn belongs to God (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: God claims every firstborn male among the Israelites, human or animal, as his own. This ties back to the night Egypt's firstborn died while Israel's were spared.

parts.label: A yearly festival of flat bread (vv. 3-10)
parts.note: Each spring, in the month of Aviv, the people were to eat bread without yeast for seven days, remembering a departure so rushed there was no time for dough to rise. Parents were to explain it to their children, and the picture of a mark on the hand and head most likely means a constant reminder, though later Jewish practice also took it literally, wearing small boxes holding these verses on the arm and head.

parts.label: Firstborn animals and sons (vv. 11-16)
parts.note: Firstborn male livestock were offered to God, while a donkey, not used for offerings, was exchanged for a lamb or killed. Firstborn sons were never sacrificed but redeemed, meaning bought back with a payment, and the ritual was meant to prompt children to ask why.

parts.label: The long way around (vv. 17-18)
parts.note: God avoided the short coastal road through Philistine territory, judging that an early battle might send the people back to Egypt. Instead they headed toward the Red Sea, called in Hebrew the Sea of Reeds, whose exact location scholars still debate.

parts.label: Joseph's bones (v. 19)
parts.note: Joseph, who had brought the family to Egypt generations earlier, made them promise to carry his remains to the land God promised. Taking his bones along keeps that old promise and links this escape to the family's earlier story.

parts.label: Cloud by day, fire by night (vv. 20-22)
parts.note: The LORD led them as a column of cloud in daytime and a column of fire at night, so they could travel at any hour. It never left its place at the front of the people.

think: What stories or rituals from your own family or culture carry a memory forward, and what might be lost if they stopped being told?
